# Studs Terkel, Chronicler of Everyday America, Dies at 96

Studs Terkel, the Pulitzer Prize-winning author, radio host, and lifelong activist who transformed the way America listened to itself, died Friday at his Chicago home. He was 96.

For more than half a century, Terkel devoted his career to a singular and revolutionary idea: that the most profound truths about a nation could be found not in the pronouncements of the powerful, but in the voices of ordinary working-class people. Through his pioneering oral histories, he gave a permanent record to the janitors, factory workers, farmers, waitresses, and countless others whose experiences had long gone unrecorded in the official chronicles of history.

His approach was rooted in his earliest years. As a boy, Terkel spent countless hours in the lobby of his parents' Chicago hotel, absorbing the conversations, arguments, and confessions of the working men and women who passed through its doors. Those childhood observations shaped a lifelong conviction that would define his work. He came to believe, as he often said, that "the oral history of the unknowns" is what truly drives history forward—that the sweep of human events is authored not by presidents and generals alone, but by the collective experiences of the anonymous many.

That philosophy found its fullest expression in his acclaimed books, in which he interviewed hundreds of Americans and wove their firsthand accounts into sprawling, intimate portraits of the national experience. His work reached its highest recognition in 1985, when he was awarded the Pulitzer Prize for *"The Good War,"* his oral history of World War II as told by those who lived through it. The prize confirmed what many had already understood: that Terkel had become synonymous with the act of capturing the voices of everyday Americans.

Beyond his books, Terkel was a fixture of Chicago radio, where his warm curiosity and gift for listening made him a beloved interviewer and a tireless champion of the causes he believed in. He remained an activist throughout his life, using his platform to advocate for the dignity of the common person.

In an era that so often celebrated the famous and the influential, Studs Terkel spent his life insisting that everyone had a story worth telling—and worth remembering. His legacy endures in the millions of words he preserved, and in the enduring reminder that history belongs, above all, to the people who live it.

# CNN and the Pulitzer Prize

## Understanding the Connection Between Broadcast Journalism and America's Most Prestigious Award

The **Pulitzer Prize** stands as one of the most respected honors in American journalism, literature, and musical composition. Established in 1917 through the will of newspaper publisher Joseph Pulitzer, the award has long recognized excellence in reporting and writing.

### A Historic Shift in Eligibility

For much of its history, the Pulitzer Prize was reserved exclusively for print-based journalism, leaving broadcast and online outlets ineligible. This meant that major networks like **CNN** (Cable News Network), founded by Ted Turner in 1980, could not traditionally compete for these awards despite their significant contributions to global news coverage.

However, the media landscape has evolved dramatically. As digital journalism blurred the lines between print and broadcast, the Pulitzer board began expanding eligibility to include online content and, eventually, audio reporting.

### CNN's Journalistic Impact

Throughout its decades of operation, **CNN** has been recognized with numerous prestigious awards, including:

- **Peabody Awards** for excellence in broadcasting
- **Emmy Awards** for outstanding news coverage
- **Edward R. Murrow Awards** for journalistic achievement

While the network has built an impressive reputation for breaking news and international reporting, the Pulitzer Prize has historically celebrated a different medium of storytelling.

### The Evolving Definition of Journalism

The relationship between organizations like CNN and awards like the Pulitzer highlights an important conversation in modern media: **how do we recognize excellence across different platforms?** As journalism continues to transform in the digital age, the boundaries between traditional categories continue to shift.

# Studs Terkel, Legendary Oral Historian and Chronicler of American Life, Dies at 96

**CHICAGO** — Studs Terkel, the Pulitzer Prize-winning author, broadcaster, and irrepressible chronicler of ordinary American lives whose tape recorder captured the voices of a century, died Friday at his home in Chicago. He was 96.

His son, Dan Terkel, confirmed the death, saying his father had never fully recovered from a fall in his home several weeks earlier. "He led a full, eventful, and sometimes tempestuous life," his son said, adding that his father had lived exactly as he wished, surrounded by the books, recordings, and conversations that defined his work.

With his rumpled appearance, ever-present cigar, and signature red-checked shirts, Terkel became one of the most recognizable figures in American letters. But it was his ear, not his eye, that made him extraordinary. Over more than half a century, he interviewed thousands of people—factory workers, jazz musicians, waitresses, doctors, gravediggers, and titans of industry—transforming their testimony into a running portrait of the American experience.

## The Voice of the Voiceless

Terkel pioneered a form of oral history that gave dignity and permanence to the everyday. His books, assembled from countless hours of recorded interviews, were built almost entirely from the words of his subjects, with Terkel serving as a self-effacing guide.

"I celebrate the non-celebrated," he once said. "The ones who are rarely, if ever, asked how they feel about their lives, their work, their hopes and their fears."

His landmark works included "Division Street: America" (1967), "Hard Times" (1970), an oral history of the Great Depression, and "Working" (1974), a sprawling examination of how Americans felt about their jobs. The latter opened with a line that became one of his most quoted observations: work, he wrote, was "about violence—to the spirit as well as to the body."

In 1985, Terkel received the Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction for "The Good War: An Oral History of World War Two." The book gathered the recollections of soldiers, civilians, and survivors, and its title carried a deliberate irony. Terkel used quotation marks around "good" to question the very notion that any war could be described as such, even one widely regarded as morally justified.

"The title is a phrase that many people use," he explained. "There's no such thing as a good war. But it was necessary. That's a different matter."

## A Philosophy of Listening

At the heart of Terkel's method was a simple but radical belief: that everyone had a story worth telling, and that history belonged as much to the anonymous as to the powerful.

"History is not just the doings of great men," he argued. "It is the accumulated experience of everyone who ever lived." He often described himself not as an interviewer but as a listener, and he insisted that the key to a good conversation was genuine curiosity rather than cleverness.

Terkel famously distrusted his own technical skills, joking about his inability to operate the tape recorder that was his most essential tool. Yet what he lacked in mechanical aptitude he made up for in empathy. Subjects who had never spoken to a journalist found themselves opening up to the disheveled man with the gravelly voice, revealing intimacies they had told no one.

"When people talk, they reveal not just facts, but feelings," he said. "And feelings are the truth of history."

## From Radio to the Page

Louis "Studs" Terkel was born on May 16, 1912, in New York City, and moved with his family to Chicago as a child. His parents ran a rooming house, and the young Terkel absorbed the conversations of the workers, drifters, and dreamers who passed through—an early education in the American vernacular that would shape his life's work.

He took his nickname from the fictional character Studs Lonigan, the protagonist of James T. Farrell's Chicago novels. Though he earned a law degree from the University of Chicago, he never practiced, drifting instead into acting, radio, and eventually the burgeoning medium of television.

His early broadcasting career was interrupted during the McCarthy era, when Terkel—an unapologetic leftist who had signed numerous progressive petitions—was blacklisted. He refused to recant his political views, a stance that cost him work but earned him a reputation for integrity that endured throughout his life.

For 45 years, beginning in 1952, Terkel hosted a daily radio program on Chicago's WFMT, interviewing an astonishing range of guests, from Bertrand Russell and Martin Luther King Jr. to unknown citizens plucked from the street. The show became an institution, and Chicago became inseparable from his identity.

## Later Years and a Final Reckoning

Terkel remained productive well into his 90s, publishing books on faith, death, and hope even as his own health declined. In 2005, he underwent successful open-heart surgery at the age of 93, quipping afterward about his determination to keep working.

In 2007, he published "Touch and Go," a memoir that looked back on his long and unlikely life. The title captured both the precariousness of his early years and the improvisational spirit that carried him through them. In it, Terkel reflected on his brushes with the blacklist, his marriage of six decades to his wife Ida, and the countless voices that had passed through his recordings.

The book was characteristically unsentimental yet deeply humane, and it doubled as a meditation on memory itself—on how a life, like a nation, is stitched together from fragments of remembered experience. Ida, his beloved wife and partner, had died in 1999, a loss that shadowed his final years even as he pressed on with his work.

Terkel often spoke of death without fear, framing it as simply another part of the human story he had spent his career documenting. He said he wanted his epitaph to read: "Curiosity did not kill this cat."

## A Lasting Legacy

Terkel's influence extended far beyond the printed page. His approach to oral history inspired generations of journalists, documentarians, and historians who sought to democratize the way the past is recorded. The StoryCorps project, which invites ordinary Americans to record conversations with loved ones, owes an explicit debt to his vision.

"Studs taught us that everybody is somebody," said one longtime admirer of his work. "He gave voice to people who thought no one was listening."

In addition to his son, Dan, Terkel is survived by grandchildren and by an archive of thousands of recorded interviews now preserved for future generations—a vast chorus of American voices, gathered by a man who believed that listening was its own form of love.

He asked, near the end of his life, to be remembered not as a great writer or broadcaster, but as something simpler.

"I was a guy who listened," he said. "That's all. I listened."
